title: Prayer: A Bible Study on Learning to Pray
subtitle: A five-session study on prayer, walking slowly through the words Jesus gave us.
summary:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and anyone who has been praying for years and quietly suspects they never learned how. It's also for people who stopped praying because the words ran out or the heavens went quiet. It walks through the prayer Jesus gave when his own disciples, who had watched him pray, asked him to teach them. It isn't a book about prayer. It's a school of prayer that runs on the words of the Lord's Prayer, one clause at a time.

The five sessions follow the prayer in order. Who we pray to, and how we dare to call him Father. What we're really asking when we ask for his name to be hallowed and his kingdom to come. The daily bread that ends our pretending we feed ourselves. The forgiveness we receive and the forgiveness we're then bound to give. And the prayer prayed in the dark, when the asking goes unanswered and the faithful thing left is to keep asking.

The study won't hand anyone a technique for getting God to perform, and the leader shouldn't either. Prayer isn't a lever. It's a child speaking to a Father, and some people in the room have no working picture of a father at all, because theirs left, or never came, or stayed and did harm. The study is written from inside the struggle with prayer, not from above it, and it asks the leader to lead from the same place.
audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

sessions.title: Our Father
sessions.aim: To begin where Jesus begins, with a name rather than a method, and to face plainly that the first word of the prayer is the hardest one for anyone whose father failed them, without falling into either a sentimental picture of God or the bitter conclusion that the word means nothing.
sessions.summary:
The disciples didn't ask Jesus for a theology lesson. They asked him to teach them to pray, and the first thing he gave them was a relationship: "Our Father." So the first question of this study isn't how to pray but to whom, because everything else depends on it.

For the person whose father walked out, or never came, or came only to do damage, that word isn't warm. It's a closed door. That has to be granted fully. But throwing the word away leaves you praying to a force, and pretending your father was fine is a lie God never asked you to tell. Jesus isn't saying God is like your father. He's saying God is the Father every earthly father was meant to reflect and didn't.

Then two small words keep the prayer in balance. It's "our," not "my," so no one prays alone. And it's "in heaven," so the One near enough to call Father is also holy. Before we ask for anything, the prayer tells us who we are.

keyScripture.why: "Pray then like this: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name" (Matthew 6:9). Jesus opens with an address, not a request. The relationship comes before the asking, and the One addressed is near enough to call Father and holy enough to hallow.

discussion.q: When you hear God called Father, what's your first reaction, before the correct one? Where do you think that reaction comes from?
discussion.behind: Get the gut response out before any teaching. For some the word is warm and for some it's a closed door, and the difference usually traces back to a human father. You're not settling anything yet, only bringing it into the open, because everyone in the room is praying to whatever picture that word calls up. Go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: Read Luke 11:1-2. The disciples asked to be taught to pray, and Jesus started with a name, not a method. Why do you think he began with who we pray to rather than how?
discussion.behind: Move the room off the reflex for technique. We come wanting a how and Jesus gives a whom. Let people feel that prayer rests on a relationship before it's shaped by any rule, so the rest of the study is a conversation with a Father and not a set of skills.

discussion.q: Some of us quietly assume God is our own father made bigger. What changes if it's the other way around, and God is the Father our fathers were meant to reflect?
discussion.behind: This is the turning point for the wounded. For some, "God is like my father, only bigger" is terrifying. Help them see the reversal: the human father was the imperfect copy, so his failures don't define God. Go gently; this can touch something raw.

discussion.q: Jesus says "our Father," not "my Father," and "in heaven," not down the hall. What does each of those keep prayer from turning into?
discussion.behind: Help the room hold both. "Our" keeps prayer from being a lonely solo act; even alone in a room you pray as one of a family. "In heaven" keeps God from becoming a buddy. Prayer is close and reverent at the same time.

discussion.q: Where have you found the word Father hard to say to God, and what have you done with that difficulty?
discussion.behind: Bring it home without hunting for a dramatic confession. Answer first and briefly. You want each person inside the question, because the gospel gives a Father especially to those who never had one. Keep it gentle, and don't press anyone who stays quiet.

objections.objection: Calling God Father is fine for people who had good fathers. For the rest of us it's cruel. You're asking me to feel safe with the very word that names the person who hurt me most, and no theology fixes that.
objections.response: This deserves to be heard all the way through, because it's true about the wound. The word can land like a blow instead of a comfort, and pretending otherwise would be a lie. But listen to the direction of what Jesus says. He isn't saying God is a bigger version of your father. He's saying the reverse. God is the Father, the original, and every earthly father, the absent one and the cruel one and even the good one, was only ever a copy, and a broken one. Your father didn't define fatherhood for God to live up to. God defined it, and your father fell short. So when you pray "our Father," you aren't handing God the face of the man who failed you. You're going past that man to the One he was supposed to show you. The word doesn't belong to your wound. It belongs to God, and he's giving it to you.

objections.objection: If I have to feel warmth toward God as Father to pray this honestly, I can't. I feel nothing. So either I'm disqualified or I have to fake an emotion I don't have.
objections.response: You're not disqualified, and you aren't asked to fake anything. Prayer doesn't begin with a feeling you produce. It begins with something you're given. Paul says believers have "received the Spirit of adoption as sons" (Romans 8:15). That's true on the mornings it feels true and on the mornings it doesn't, because it rests on what God has done. A few verses later Paul says that when we don't know what to pray, "the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words" (Romans 8:26). So say the word before you feel it, the way a child learns a name he didn't grow up hearing. If the feeling comes, it can come later. What God has done carries the prayer when the feeling can't.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If God really is the Father your own father was meant to show you, what's the one thing you've always wanted to hear a father say and never have?
sessions.practice: This week, pray only the first two words: "Our Father." Don't rush past them to your requests. Each day, say them slowly a few times and notice what comes up, whether it's warmth, or nothing, or a flinch. Don't judge it. If the word is hard, say it anyway, the way a child learns a name. At the end of the week, write down whether saying it changed how the rest of your prayers felt.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, some of us say that word easily, and some of us say it through clenched teeth, because the man it should have named let us down or was never there. You know which of us is which. Thank you that you aren't a copy of our fathers but the Father they were meant to show us, and that you've made us your children because you chose to, not because we earned it. Teach the fatherless among us, and there are more of us than we admit, that we have a Father in heaven. Hallowed be your name. Amen.
reflection: What picture of a father do I bring to God without realizing it, and how has it shaped the way I pray, or kept me from praying?
Where have I assumed God is my earthly father made bigger, when my earthly father was only ever a broken copy of him?
If I really am adopted, a child of God whether or not it feels true today, what would change about how I come to him this week?
sessions.teaching:
The disciples had watched Jesus pray. Luke tells us he slipped away to pray before major turns in his life, that he spent a whole night in prayer before choosing the twelve (Luke 6:12), and one day, when he finished praying, one of them said, "Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples" (Luke 11:1). They didn't ask him to teach them about prayer. They asked him to teach them to pray. And notice what he doesn't give them. There's no posture, no method, no list of techniques. He gives them a relationship in the first words out of his mouth: "Our Father in heaven" (Matthew 6:9). Before there's a single request, before kingdom or bread or forgiveness, there's an address. The first question of prayer was never how. It was always to whom.

That's where the hardest objection comes in, and for many people in any room it isn't theoretical. Calling God Father is a comfort if you had a good father. If you didn't, it's a wound. For the person whose father walked out, or never showed up, or showed up only to do damage, the word is a locked door, and being told to pray it can feel like being told to feel safe with the name of the person who taught you that men leave. I was raised without a father, so I'm not going to wave that away.

But here's what changes things. Jesus isn't saying God is like your father. That's the assumption that frightens the wounded: that God is your earthly father made enormous, the same absence or the same temper with more power behind it. Jesus is saying the opposite. God is the Father, the original. Every human father who ever lived, the one who left and the one who stayed and even the rare good one, was a copy, and a broken copy at that. Your father didn't set the standard that God then had to meet. God set it, and your father fell short of it, the way every image falls short of what it was made to show. Long before Jesus, a psalm called God "Father of the fatherless" (Psalm 68:5). The name was always aimed at the people who needed it most.

So when you pray "our Father," you aren't giving the man who failed you a bigger title. You're going over his head to the One he was supposed to show you and didn't. The word doesn't belong to your wound. It belongs to God, and the astonishing thing about the gospel is that he hands it to the very people who never got to use it. Paul says we've "received the Spirit of adoption as sons" (Romans 8:15). The right to say Father isn't something we're born with or something we feel our way into. It's given.

Now look at the two words around it, because they hold the prayer in balance. It's "our" Father, not "my" Father. Jesus won't let prayer become a private performance between me and God. It's a family word. Even alone in a room, you pray as one of a people, joined to everyone else saying the same name, so the loneliest person praying isn't alone. And it's our Father "in heaven," not a tame God down the hall who's there to indulge us. "In heaven" keeps him holy. The One near enough to be called Father is also high enough that the next words are "hallowed be your name."

We need both. Keller's book on prayer is subtitled Experiencing Awe and Intimacy with God, and that pairing is exactly right. Take away the heaven and you get sentimentality, a God too soft to save anyone. Take away the Father and you get dread, a God too far off to reach. A wounded heart usually swings to one side or the other. It either makes God small and manageable, or it makes him the absent father with infinite power. Neither is the God of this prayer.

So before we ask for anything, notice what's already happened. The first thing this prayer does isn't change God's mind. It tells you who you are. Before you bring him a single need, he's named you his child. If you came tonight unsure you have any standing to pray, unsure the word Father means anything when you say it, the standing was never yours to earn. It was given in Christ, who makes the fatherless into sons and daughters. Say the word before you feel it, the way a child learns a name he never got to use, and let the real Father teach you, slowly, what it was always meant to mean.

scriptureStudy.note: "Pray then like this: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name." The address comes before any request. Prayer rests on a relationship, and the relationship is a family one, near enough for "Father" and high enough for "hallowed."

"Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples." They'd watched him pray and wanted what he had. They asked to be taught, which means prayer is learned. Even the disciples didn't assume they already knew how.

Believers have "received the Spirit of adoption as sons," and by the Spirit they cry out to God as Father. The right to call God Father isn't natural to us. It's given in adoption, and even the cry is the Spirit's work.

"God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts," crying out to God as Father. The closeness is the Spirit's gift, not our achievement, so the fatherless can say the word truly. It's supplied by God's Spirit, not by our history.
"Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation." Long before Jesus, God claimed the name for those who had no father.

"But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him." Jesus' own picture of the Father is a father who runs toward the child coming home, the opposite of the distant or punishing father many people fear.
"See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are." Adoption isn't a thin metaphor. It's a real new standing, named by the Father himself.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, look at how carefully the early church guarded the word Father. In parts of the ancient church the Lord's Prayer was taught to new believers as they came to baptism, and prayed as the prayer of those entering God's family. Calling God Father was treated as the privilege of the adopted, not something every creature could assume. Set that beside the common modern assumption that everyone everywhere is a child of God in the same sense, and ask what's gained and what's lost when the word is flattened. The older view made the word precious because it was a gift.

Then consider how the Reformers and those who follow them, Keller among them, have spoken of adoption as one of the high points of salvation: not only forgiven but welcomed into the family, not only acquitted but named. For the fatherless, adoption isn't an abstraction. It's the very thing they lacked and longed for, and the gospel offers it at the center, not as a consolation prize. Ask the group how to hold the word Father as both holy and tender, neither so reverent it goes cold nor so familiar it goes cheap, remembering that for some in the room it's the hardest word in the prayer.

memoryVerse.text: Pray then like this: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name.

sessions.title: Hallowed Be Your Name, Your Kingdom Come
sessions.aim: To see that the first things Jesus teaches us to ask for are God's honor and God's reign, not our needs, and that this order isn't God's vanity but the cure for ours: prayer as the slow reordering of a heart toward what's actually worth wanting.
sessions.summary:
We come to prayer with a list, and the list starts with us. Jesus teaches a prayer whose first three requests are about God, his name, his kingdom, his will, and only then turns to our bread. Why would a Father who already knows what we need have us ask first for his name to be honored?

The suspicion is worth stating fairly: a God who wants praise first sounds insecure, an ego needing applause before he'll attend to the help we came for. But that misreads what hallowing is for. God doesn't need his name honored. We need to honor it, because a heart that puts anything else first is already breaking on the wrong center.

"Your kingdom come" is no safer. It isn't a request for a better version of my plans. It's a prayer for a different king, and it asks God to take the throne I've been sitting on. Prayer isn't first about getting what I want. It's about being given new wants.

keyScripture.why: "Hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven" (Matthew 6:9-10). God's honor, reign, and will come before any request of ours, and prayer becomes the reordering of desire toward what is first in reality instead of what is first on our list.

discussion.q: Be honest about your own prayers. What tends to come first, God's name and kingdom or your needs and wants? What does the order tell you?
discussion.behind: Bring our usual order into the open before judging it. Most of us start with our list, and naming that is the beginning. You're after recognition, not guilt. Jesus reverses the order we walk in with, and the reversal is the point of the session.

discussion.q: Some people hear "hallowed be your name" and think God sounds insecure, wanting praise before he'll help. What's right about that instinct, and what does it miss?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. The instinct rightly recoils from a needy God. What it misses is that hallowing is for our sake, the retraining of a heart that breaks when it centers on anything else. Help the room move from "God needs praise" to "we need to praise."

discussion.q: Read Matthew 6:8 and 6:33. If the Father already knows what we need, what is the asking for? What does "seek first" ask of you?
discussion.behind: Jesus says just before the prayer that the Father knows what we need before we ask. So the asking isn't to inform God. It forms the one praying. Matthew 6:33 puts the same order into a command. Let the group connect the two.

discussion.q: Where in your life is something other than God sitting in first place, and how is that working out?
discussion.behind: Press gently on disordered desire. We all crown something, money, approval, a person, control, and call it normal. You want people to recognize the wrong center, not a contest of confessions, so that people feel why the petition is mercy and not vanity.

discussion.q: We sometimes pray "your kingdom come" while hoping God will fund ours. Where do you ask God to bless your plans rather than to replace them with his?
discussion.behind: Answer first. Most of our kingdom prayers are requests for God to sponsor our own agenda. You aren't trying to resolve this, only to see it: we keep asking God to serve our kingdom while saying the words of his.

objections.objection: A God who insists you praise his name before he'll help you sounds like a fragile ego, not a loving Father. Why would the Maker of the universe need me to tell him how great he is before he listens to my problem?
objections.response: The instinct behind this is healthy. A God who needed our applause to feel secure wouldn't be worth praying to. But hallowing isn't for God's sake. It's for ours. He gains nothing when his name is honored, the way a mountain gains nothing when you admire it. You're the one who gains. The human heart always puts something first, and when that first thing can't bear the weight, the heart cracks under it. To pray "hallowed be your name" is to ask God to fix that, to make first in me what's actually first, so I stop worshiping things that will crush me. He isn't fishing for compliments. He's healing the disordered love behind so much of our misery.

objections.objection: Praying "your kingdom come, your will be done" sounds like resignation: whatever happens must be God's will, so why try to change anything?
objections.response: The words themselves say the opposite. "On earth as it is in heaven" (Matthew 6:10) names a gap between the world as God means it to be and the world as it is, and asks for that gap to close. That's a deeply dissatisfied prayer, not a resigned one. The prophets refused to treat injustice as the weather, and this petition carries their refusal. You can't really pray for God's kingdom to come and then settle comfortably into the way things are. The prayer makes you restless, and in the right direction.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If you're honest, what's actually in first place in your heart this week, and what would it mean to ask God to put his name there instead?
sessions.practice: This week, spend the first minute of each prayer only on God: his name, his character, what's true of him whatever your circumstances. Don't ask for anything yet. Then, when you bring your requests, hold each one up to a question: am I asking God to bless my kingdom or to bring his? Write down what you notice when you put his name first on purpose, and whether your asking changed.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we come to you with our lists, and our lists begin with us, and we've called that normal so long we no longer notice. Forgive us for the small kingdoms we run badly and defend hard, and for asking you to pay for them. Hallowed be your name, not because you need our praise but because we need to give it, and our hearts break on every other center. Your kingdom come, even into the places we've been ruling. Reorder what we want until we want you first. On earth as it is in heaven. Amen.
reflection: What's sitting in first place in my heart, and how is that coming out as anxiety, anger, or exhaustion?
What does the small kingdom I run look like, and what would it cost me to pray for God's to replace it?
Where am I asking God to bless my plans when I should be asking him for new ones?
sessions.teaching:
If we're honest, the list we bring to prayer begins with us: our needs, our fears, our people, our plans, whatever kept us up last night. That isn't wicked. It's human, and Jesus doesn't condemn it. But watch the order of the prayer he teaches. The first three requests aren't about us at all. "Hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven" (Matthew 6:9-10). Only after God's name, God's reign, and God's will does the prayer turn to our bread, our debts, and our temptations. It reverses the order we walk in with.

Why would it? Just a verse earlier Jesus says, "your Father knows what you need before you ask him" (Matthew 6:8). So why make us begin by asking for his name to be honored? If we're honest, it can sound a little like vanity. We've all known people who need to be told how great they are before they'll help, and we don't enjoy their company. A God like that would hardly be worth the breath. That instinct is right about one thing.

But it misreads what hallowing is for, and getting this right opens the whole prayer. God doesn't need his name hallowed. You need to hallow it. Your honor adds nothing to him, the way your admiration adds nothing to a mountain and your refusal subtracts nothing from its height. The hallowing isn't for the mountain. It's for the person looking at it.

Here's the truth about the human heart this petition is meant to heal. The heart always crowns something. It always has a first thing it organizes the rest of life around, and whatever sits there is what it worships, whatever we call it. Augustine opened his Confessions by telling God that our heart is restless until it rests in him, and elsewhere he described sin as disordered love: loving good things in the wrong order, putting lesser things where only God belongs. Most of us, most of the time, have something in that first place that can't bear the weight. It might be money, or what people think of us, or a relationship, or our own control. A heart built on a center that can't hold is always, quietly, breaking.

To pray "hallowed be your name" is to ask God for the one thing that heals that. It asks him to make first in me what's actually first, to take the throne of my wanting away from the things that crush me and put his name there, where my heart was made to rest. That isn't flattery he demands; it's mercy he offers.

Then comes "your kingdom come," and it isn't safe either, though we say it as if it were. We hear it as a vague hope that things will improve, ideally along lines we already like. But a kingdom has a king, and to pray for God's kingdom is to pray for a different king than the one currently ruling my life, who is usually me. Every one of us runs a small kingdom. We have our territory, our preferences, our will done, and we defend it hard and rule it badly. Praying "your kingdom come" is quietly a kind of treason against my own rule.

"On earth as it is in heaven" tells you what we're asking for. It names a gap between the world as God intends it and the world as it is. Walter Brueggemann has written about the prophetic imagination, the refusal to accept that the way things are is the way they must be. This petition carries that refusal. It isn't a shrug; it's the most dissatisfied prayer there is, and you can't mean it and then settle comfortably into the world as it is.

I have to say where this breaks down, because I'm in it too. We pray "your kingdom come" and quietly hope God will fund ours instead. We pray "hallowed be your name" and then spend the day building our own. We ask him to bless our plans when the prayer asks him to replace them. That turns God into a chaplain for our kingdom. Prayer isn't first about getting what I want. It's about being given new wants. We come to change our circumstances, and Jesus gives us a prayer that begins by changing our desires. Put his name first, and the wanting starts to heal. Seek his kingdom first, and your small one loosens its grip.

scriptureStudy.note: "Hallowed be your name." The first request is about God, and it isn't flattery he needs. It's a reordering we need, asking that his name hold the first place in us that it already holds in reality.

"Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven." A kingdom means a king, so this is a prayer for a reign other than our own. "On earth as it is in heaven" names the gap we're asking God to close.
"Your Father knows what you need before you ask him." Jesus says this just before the prayer. The asking isn't to inform God. It forms the one who prays.
"But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you." The same order as the prayer: the kingdom sought first, and our needs trusted to follow.

"One thing have I asked of the LORD, that will I seek after: that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life." A heart with one first thing, which is what hallowing his name slowly produces in us.
"Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts." Isaiah's vision of heaven is the unending hallowing of God's name. When we pray "hallowed be your name," we ask for that to spread to earth.

"The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever." The end of the story answers "your kingdom come": the gap closed and every rival throne empty.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, take up Augustine's account of disordered love, because it sits underneath this session and has shaped Christian thinking about desire for sixteen centuries. On his account, sin is less the love of bad things than loving good things in the wrong order, lesser goods above greater ones and created things above the Creator. The problem isn't that we want too much but that we want wrongly, and the cure isn't killing desire but putting it back in order, with God first. Set that beside the modern assumption that what I want simply is who I am and can't be questioned, and ask what's lost when we stop believing our wants can be wrong and can be retrained.

Then connect it to James K. A. Smith's argument in You Are What You Love that we're shaped less by what we think than by what we love, and that our loves are formed by habits and repeated practices. Daily prayer is one of them. On that view, praying "hallowed be your name" isn't only a sentiment but a practice that slowly reorders the heart. Ask the group which daily habits are already training their loves, and in which direction.
