sessions.title: Give Us This Day
sessions.aim: To hear the request for daily bread as the end of the self-made life, a prayer that admits we can't keep ourselves alive, and to face why a self-sufficient culture finds dependence so hard to bear while a praying heart finds in it the beginning of rest.
sessions.summary:
After three requests about God, the prayer turns to us, and the first thing it asks for is bread. Not success or a calling or great things. Bread, the plainest need there is, and only for today. Why would Jesus have us ask for what most of us can simply buy?

The modern objection is fair: we have paychecks and grocery stores, and praying for food we can purchase can feel like a leftover from a peasant economy. We can buy it. But the petition isn't mainly about the bread. It's about who we think keeps us alive. To pray it is to admit that we're creatures, that the breath in our lungs and the food on the table come from a hand that isn't ours.

"This day" and "daily" matter too. The prayer won't let us secure tomorrow. It echoes the manna that spoiled when it was hoarded. Self-sufficiency is a story we tell until the diagnosis comes or the job ends, and dependence isn't the failure of a strong life. It's the truth a strong life was hiding.

keyScripture.why: "Give us this day our daily bread" (Matthew 6:11). We ask God for the most basic need, and only for today's portion. The prayer names us as creatures who don't keep ourselves alive and refuses the self-sufficiency that hoards against tomorrow.

discussion.q: Jesus teaches us to ask God for bread, which most of us can just buy. Why do you think he has us ask for what we're able to provide ourselves?
discussion.behind: Start with how strange the request feels. We don't think we need to pray for food we can purchase, and that very feeling is the target. Bring our assumed self-sufficiency into the open, so the room can feel that the asking is about knowing the source, not telling God about a shortage.

discussion.q: When has your own sense of self-sufficiency cracked, through illness, a lost job, or a loss, and what did the crack show you?
discussion.behind: Most people have had a moment when the feeling of control broke, and that's where dependence stops being an idea. Go gently; some of these wounds are fresh. You're after the recognition that we were always dependent and the crisis only showed it.

discussion.q: Read Exodus 16:4 and 16:19-20. Why do you think the manna spoiled when people kept it overnight? What does that suggest about why Jesus says "this day"?
discussion.behind: Let the story carry it. The manna was given a day at a time, and hoarding it out of distrust didn't work. Help the room see that asking for today is a discipline against the anxiety of trying to secure a tomorrow we can't control.

discussion.q: Where is it hardest for you to admit that you depend on God, and why does admitting it feel like weakness?
discussion.behind: Get at the shame around need. We're trained to see dependence as failure and independence as virtue. You want people to see that admitting we don't keep ourselves alive isn't weakness but plain truth, and the beginning of rest.

discussion.q: Many of us pray "give us this day" and then live as if we'd secured the next ten years. Where do you say words of dependence while building a life of self-sufficiency?
discussion.behind: Answer first and name the gap in your own life. We pray for daily bread and then store, insure, and control as if everything depended on us. You're not trying to resolve the contradiction tonight, only to see it.

objections.objection: Praying for daily bread is a relic from before grocery stores. I have a paycheck and a refrigerator. Asking God for food I can buy is either pretending to be poorer than I am or going through a meaningless motion.
objections.response: You can buy the bread, and the prayer doesn't ask you to pretend you can't. But it was never mainly about the bread. It's about who you believe keeps you alive. You didn't make the wheat grow. You didn't give yourself the strength to earn the paycheck. You didn't make your heart beat this morning, and you can't guarantee it will beat tonight. The grocery store doesn't change the fact that you're a creature. It hides it behind a long supply chain. To pray "give us this day our daily bread" is to look past the chain to the source and admit that the whole arrangement is a gift. The prayer isn't asking you to feel poor. It's asking you to stop pretending you're self-made.

objections.objection: If I'm supposed to trust God for daily bread and not worry about tomorrow, am I being irresponsible to save and plan for my family's future? Is this prayer telling me to live hand to mouth and call it faith?
objections.response: No, and Scripture is careful here, so we should be too. The same Bible that gives us this prayer points to the ant that "prepares her bread in summer" (Proverbs 6:8) and says that anyone who doesn't provide for his household has denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8). Daily bread doesn't forbid planning. It forbids trusting the plan, the quiet belief that your savings, and not God, are what really keep you. You can save and plan and provide while admitting every morning that your security isn't finally in the savings but in the Giver, who can hold you when the savings are gone. Work, provide, plan, and hold it all with an open hand.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What have you been trusting to keep you safe instead of God, the savings, the plan, the control, and what would it mean to ask him for just today's portion?
sessions.practice: This week, pray for your daily bread every morning before the day's plans take over. Ask God for just this day, and say out loud that you can't keep yourself alive. Once during the week, take something you usually check to feel secure, your bank balance, your calendar, your to-do list, and instead of looking to it for reassurance, pray over it and hand the security back to the Giver. Write down what it stirred in you to ask for only today.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we've built lives designed so that we never have to ask you for bread, and we've called that maturity. We didn't grow the wheat. We didn't give ourselves the strength to work or the breath to wake. Forgive us for a self-sufficiency that's really dependence with the source hidden. Give us this day our daily bread, and teach us to trust you one day at a time, the way you fed your people one morning at a time in the wilderness. When our plans fail, and they will, let us find that you were holding us all along. Amen.
reflection: Where have I hidden my dependence behind a paycheck and a full pantry, and called myself self-made?
When my self-sufficiency has cracked, through loss or illness or failure, what did the crack show me that the strong years had hidden?
What would it mean to ask God for only this day, and to hold my plans and savings with an open hand?
sessions.teaching:
After three requests lifted toward God, the prayer comes down to earth, and the first thing it asks for us is almost shockingly small. "Give us this day our daily bread" (Matthew 6:11). Not a calling, not success, not rescue from our enemies, not great spiritual things. Bread, the plainest need a body has, the thing a peasant and a king both require. So why does Jesus teach us to ask God for the one thing nearly everyone in this room can provide for themselves? We don't lie awake wondering if there'll be food tomorrow. We have refrigerators and paychecks and a store a few minutes away.

The objection deserves its full weight. Praying for daily bread made obvious sense when a failed harvest meant a buried child. Now bread is a purchase, not a hope, and asking God for it can feel like pretending to be poorer than you are. The bread really is there; you really can buy it.

But the prayer was never mainly about the bread. It's about who you believe keeps you alive. You can buy the food, but you didn't make the wheat grow or send the rain. You didn't give yourself the strength to work or the mind to do your job or the body that has, so far, kept going. You didn't make your heart beat this morning, and you can't guarantee it will beat tonight. The grocery store didn't end your dependence. It hid it, behind a supply chain so long and reliable that you forgot you were being fed. To pray for daily bread is to look past the chain to its source and say out loud what the self-made life is built to deny: I'm a creature. Every bite and every breath is a gift.

Our culture is very good at helping us forget this. We're taught from childhood that dependence is failure and independence is virtue, that the goal of a life is to need no one and build something so secure you never have to ask. Charles Taylor has described the modern self as "buffered," sealed off and self-contained. We call it maturity; Scripture calls it an illusion.

Notice the second strange thing about the petition: "this day," and "daily." Jesus doesn't teach us to ask for a stockpile. He teaches us to ask for today, knowing we'll have to ask again tomorrow. That echoes the manna in the wilderness. God told Moses, "I am about to rain bread from heaven for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day's portion every day" (Exodus 16:4). Some people kept it overnight anyway, "and it bred worms and stank" (Exodus 16:20). God was training them in a trust that didn't reach past today, and he's training us. The anxious heart always wants to get far enough ahead that it never has to depend again, and this prayer won't let it. It gives us today's bread and tells us to come back tomorrow.

None of this forbids planning. Proverbs praises the ant that stores up food in summer, and Paul says a believer must provide for his household. What the prayer forbids is trusting the plan, believing the stockpile is what really keeps us. Jesus told of a rich man who tore down his barns to build bigger ones and settled in for years of ease, and God said to him, "This night your soul is required of you" (Luke 12:20). The man's mistake wasn't having a harvest. It was forgetting whose it was.

The truth is hard before it's freeing. We're allowed to believe in our self-sufficiency right up until it shatters, and for everyone it does. The diagnosis comes, the job ends, the body that always worked stops working. The person we thought would always be there is gone. And in that moment we find out what was true all along: the strength was on loan, and the bread was always daily and always a gift. We simply had enough of a cushion to pretend otherwise.

Most of us are as guilty of this as anyone. I pray for daily bread in the morning and then live as though I've personally secured the next ten years. We say the words of creatures and live like little gods. So the freedom this petition offers is the freedom to stop that exhausting pretense. You don't have to keep yourself alive. You never could. There's a hand that grows the wheat and gives the strength and keeps the heart beating, and it's the hand of a Father who gives bread to his children. Jesus went further still: "I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger" (John 6:35). Ask him for today. Tomorrow, ask again.

scriptureStudy.note: "Give us this day our daily bread." A request for the most basic need, and only for today. It names us as creatures who don't keep ourselves alive and teaches us to trust one day at a time.

"I am about to rain bread from heaven for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day's portion every day." The manna is the picture behind the petition: God feeding his people daily and training them to depend on him rather than hoard.
"Some left part of it till the morning, and it bred worms and stank." Storing up against tomorrow out of distrust didn't work. The bread was meant to be daily.

God "humbled you and let you hunger and fed you with manna... that he might make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but man lives by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD." The hunger itself was instruction, teaching a dependence a full pantry would have hidden.

"Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the food that is needful for me, lest I be full and deny you." Agur asks for daily bread, knowing that too much can breed the self-sufficiency that forgets God.
"I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger." Jesus takes the petition deeper. The daily asking points past the food to the One who is himself what we need.

The rich man built bigger barns, and God said, "This night your soul is required of you" (Luke 12:20). The parable exposes the stockpiling heart: a man who secured tomorrow and never once remembered he was a creature living on borrowed time.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, take up the old Christian teaching on creatureliness. Many theologians have taught that God doesn't simply start the world and step back but holds every creature in being at every moment, so your next breath is as much his gift as your first. Set that beside the modern ideal of the self-made individual who owes nothing to anyone, an ideal so deep in us that need feels like shame. Charles Taylor, in A Secular Age, traces how the modern self came to imagine itself as "buffered," sealed off from any sense of being held by something larger. Ask the group how much of our anxiety comes from carrying a weight, the weight of keeping ourselves going, that was never ours to carry.

Then look at the Sabbath, the weekly command to stop producing and acquiring and to receive a day as a gift (Exodus 20:8-11). Eugene Peterson wrote often against the hurry of modern life and for prayer as answering a God who speaks first. Ask what it would look like for the group to practice daily bread not only in words but in a weekly stop, and what they'd have to trust to do it.

memoryVerse.text: Give us this day our daily bread.

sessions.title: Forgive Us, As We Forgive
sessions.aim: To stand at the hinge of the prayer, the one petition Jesus comes back to and underlines, and to hold together the mercy we receive as pure gift and the mercy we're then bound to give, without softening either the cost of being forgiven or the call to forgive.
sessions.summary:
There's one petition Jesus won't leave alone. It's the only one with a condition attached, and the moment the prayer ends he comes back to explain it: "Forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors" (Matthew 6:12). Here the mercy we receive from God turns into the mercy we owe each other.

The hard question is whether God's forgiveness of me depends on my forgiveness of others. For a deeply wounded person, the clause can feel like a second injury: forgive the unforgivable or be unforgiven. That fear deserves care. But the "as" isn't a price. It shows whether mercy has landed. A forgiven heart forgives, not to earn the forgiveness but because it has been forgiven.

Forgiveness isn't pretending the wound didn't happen, and it isn't waiting to feel like it. It's bearing a real debt instead of making the other person pay it, which is what the cross was. It always costs the one who forgives. This session asks the most care of the leader, because someone in the room is carrying a wound this word will press on.

keyScripture.why: "And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors" (Matthew 6:12). The one petition Jesus underlines after the prayer ties the mercy we receive to the mercy we give, not as a transaction that earns grace but as the sign that grace has arrived.

discussion.q: Read Matthew 6:12-15. Of all the petitions, this is the only one Jesus comes back to explain after the prayer ends. Why do you think he gives forgiveness that extra weight?
discussion.behind: Start by noticing the emphasis itself. Jesus underlines this one alone, which tells us it's the hinge of the prayer, where mercy received becomes mercy given. Ask why it needed the extra warning.

discussion.q: Be honest about the word "as." Does "forgive us as we forgive" sound to you like grace received freely, or like mercy you have to earn by being merciful first?
discussion.behind: Name the fear directly; many people carry it without saying it. Stay here long enough for the room to feel the difficulty before you offer an answer, so that the answer, that the "as" shows whether mercy has landed rather than paying for it, actually lands.

discussion.q: Read Matthew 18:23-35. What's the real horror of the servant who was forgiven a fortune and then grabbed a fellow servant over a small debt?
discussion.behind: The point isn't that he broke a rule. It's that he never grasped what had been done for him. Let the group see that this is the logic of the petition: a heart that has really felt forgiven starts to loosen its grip on others' debts.

discussion.q: If forgiveness isn't pretending the wound didn't happen, and isn't waiting until you feel like it, but bearing a real debt yourself, how does that change what you thought forgiveness required of you?
discussion.behind: Correct the two common distortions, denial and feeling. Free people who thought forgiveness meant minimizing the harm or summoning an emotion. It's harder and truer than both, and it doesn't ask anyone to pretend the debt wasn't real or to put themselves back in danger.

discussion.q: Many of us pray "forgive us" while keeping a private ledger of what others owe us. Where are you keeping a ledger?
discussion.behind: This is the most exposing question in the study, so answer first and name your own ledger. You're after recognition, not pressure on the deeply wounded to forgive on a schedule. Protect anyone who has been seriously harmed; say again that forgiveness isn't the same as trust or reconciliation.

objections.objection: If God only forgives me as much as I forgive others, then grace is a transaction and the deeply wounded are trapped. You're telling abuse victims to forgive their abusers or stay unforgiven, which is a second cruelty on top of the first.
objections.response: Read as a transaction, the clause would be monstrous, and no one should be allowed to read it that way. The "as" isn't a price you pay to earn God's mercy. It's a sign of whether his mercy has reached you. A heart that has been forgiven starts to forgive the way ice in the sun starts to drip, not to cause the warmth but because of it. So a heart that claims to have received an ocean of mercy and still clutches a permanent grudge has reason to ask whether it has understood the ocean. That's very different from telling a wounded person to produce forgiveness on demand. And forgiveness isn't saying the harm was acceptable, or handing trust back to someone who hasn't changed, or staying in danger. It's the slow release of your claim to make them pay, which the deeply wounded may approach over years, with help. God is patient with that slowness.

objections.objection: Forgiveness lets the guilty off the hook. If I forgive what was done to me, I'm saying it didn't matter and giving up the justice I'm owed. Why should the one who was hurt pay the cost?
objections.response: Forgiveness doesn't say the wound didn't matter. It says the opposite: the debt is real, which is why someone has to bear it. It isn't erasing a debt as if it never existed. It's the forgiver choosing to carry the cost instead of extracting it. Yes, that's unfair, because the innocent party pays. But that unfairness is the shape of the cross, where the one who owed nothing bore what the guilty owed. Forgiveness doesn't cancel justice. You can still tell the truth, report a crime, and keep your distance. What you lay down is the personal claim to make them pay. Bonhoeffer called grace that costs nothing cheap grace, and he called it the deadly enemy of the church. Real forgiveness costs the one who forgives.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Who is the one person you haven't been able, or willing, to forgive, and what would it cost you to begin letting go of your claim to make them pay?
sessions.practice: This week, take the two halves of the petition in order, and don't skip the first. Each day, sit with what God has forgiven you, named specifically, until the size of that mercy feels real and not abstract. Only then, out of that, name one debt someone owes you and take one real step toward releasing it. It might be as small as praying for that person by name without adding a complaint. If the wound is deep, the step may be only the willingness to begin, and that counts. Forgiving doesn't mean going back into danger. Write down whether receiving mercy first changed your grip on the grudge.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we ask you to forgive us, and we mean it, and then we walk out and keep a careful record of what others owe us, and we don't see the contradiction until you show it to us. Forgive us our debts, the real ones, including the ones we've stopped noticing. Let the size of that mercy become real to us, real enough that our own grudges begin to thaw. For the deeply wounded among us, for whom forgiveness is a long road and not a single step, be patient, walk it with them, and don't let anyone rush or shame them. You bore our debt on a cross. Teach us, slowly, to bear the debts of others. Amen.
reflection: How real to me is the size of what God has forgiven me, and does the vagueness of my own forgiveness help explain how hard I find it to forgive?
Where am I asking God for mercy with one hand while demanding payment from someone with the other?
What's the difference between forgiving a wound and pretending it didn't happen, and how might naming the debt honestly help me release it?
sessions.teaching:
There's one petition in this prayer that Jesus won't leave alone. Of the five requests, it's the only one with a condition attached, and the moment the prayer is finished he comes back to explain it: "For if you forgive others their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you, but if you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses" (Matthew 6:14-15). This is the hinge of the prayer, where the mercy that comes down from God to me turns and becomes the mercy that goes from me to the person who wronged me. "Forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors" (Matthew 6:12).

The hard question has frightened sincere people for a long time. Does God's forgiveness of me depend on my forgiving others? Is mercy a wage I earn by being merciful first? For some people this isn't a puzzle. It's a wound. Read as a transaction, the clause would mean that the person who suffered most, the abused child or the betrayed spouse, has to forgive the unforgivable or lose God's forgiveness, a second cruelty on top of the first. I won't soften how that feels, and I won't let that reading stand, because it's a misreading.

The "as" isn't a price; it's a sign. Jesus isn't saying, "Forgive others so that God will forgive you," as if your mercy purchased his. He's saying the two are bound so tightly that the absence of one reveals the absence of the other. A forgiven heart forgives. That's what forgiven hearts do, the way ice brought into the sun starts to drip. It doesn't drip to earn the sun. It drips because it's been warmed.

Jesus told a story to show it. A servant owed his king a debt he could never repay, and the king forgave all of it. The same servant went out, found a fellow servant who owed him a small sum, and seized him by the throat. When the king heard, he called him back: "Should not you have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?" (Matthew 18:33). The horror of the story isn't that the man broke a rule. It's that he never grasped what had been done for him. That's the "as." Not a transaction. A window.

Now we need to be precise about what forgiveness is, because two distortions trap good people. The first says forgiveness means pretending the wound didn't happen, calling the harm acceptable, saying it was fine when it wasn't. That isn't forgiveness. It's denial, and it leaves the wound to fester. The second says forgiveness is a feeling you have to summon, so until warmth arrives you haven't done it. That leaves the wounded waiting for an emotion that may never come and blaming themselves for its absence.

Forgiveness is neither of those. It starts by naming the debt as real: the harm was genuine, the wrong was wrong. Then it chooses not to make the other person pay what they truly owe. The debt doesn't disappear. Someone bears it, and in forgiveness it's the one who was wronged. That's why it's so hard, and why it isn't fair. And it's the shape of the cross. From the cross Jesus prayed, "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do" (Luke 23:34), and there the only one who owed nothing bore what we owed and couldn't pay. Bonhoeffer called forgiveness without cost "cheap grace," grace that demands nothing and bears nothing, and he called it the deadly enemy of the church. Real forgiveness always costs the one who forgives.

Forgiveness also isn't reconciliation, and it isn't handing trust back to someone who hasn't changed. It doesn't mean staying in danger or keeping quiet about a crime. You can forgive and still tell the truth, still seek justice, still keep your distance. What you lay down is your personal claim to make them pay.

I'm the unforgiving servant more often than I'd like to admit, and I suspect most of us are. We pray "forgive us our debts" sincerely, and then walk out and keep a careful private ledger of every slight and every person who hasn't paid yet. I ask God for an ocean and ration out drops.

So hold both halves without softening either. The mercy you've received is free, a debt God himself bore at the cost of his Son, and you did nothing to deserve it. Because it's that, it can't stay inside you and leave you unchanged. A heart that has felt the size of its own forgiveness slowly loosens its grip on the debts of others, not as a payment but as a thaw. For the deeply wounded, that thaw may take years and may need help, and it may begin as nothing more than the willingness to begin. God is patient with the slowness, and so should we be. We've been forgiven much; we're learning, slowly, to forgive.

scriptureStudy.note: "And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors." The petition treats sin as a debt, something really owed, and ties the mercy we receive to the mercy we give.

"If you forgive others their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you, but if you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses." Jesus comes back to this petition alone. An unforgiving heart reveals one that hasn't taken in forgiveness; it's a sign, not a sale.

The servant forgiven a vast debt who seizes a fellow servant over a small one. The king's question, "Should not you have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?" (Matthew 18:33), is the logic of the whole petition.
"As the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive." Our forgiving flows from and takes its shape from Christ's forgiving of us.

"Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you." Forgiveness rests on the cross, not on the worthiness of the one forgiven, so the forgiver doesn't have to wait for the offender to earn it.
"Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." Jesus forgives from the cross, while bearing the wrong, not by denying that any wrong was done.

"If you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand? But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared." God doesn't keep the record against us that we're tempted to keep against others.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, read the opening chapter of Bonhoeffer's The Cost of Discipleship (1937), where he sets cheap grace against costly grace. Cheap grace, as he describes it, is forgiveness treated as a general principle that costs nothing and asks nothing. Costly grace cost God the life of his Son and calls the one who receives it to follow Christ. Set that beside a common modern account of forgiveness that reduces it to a feeling we produce for our own peace of mind, and ask what's lost when forgiveness is cut loose from the reality of the debt and the cost of bearing it.

Then weigh the hard pastoral history. Forgiveness has been used as a weapon against the abused, to pressure people back into danger and to silence true complaints. Any faithful teaching has to say clearly that forgiveness isn't reconciliation, isn't restored trust for someone who hasn't repented, and isn't giving up justice or safety. It's laying down the personal claim to make the offender pay, and it can stand alongside reporting a crime, keeping distance, and naming the wrong plainly. Ask the group where they've seen forgiveness taught too cheaply, and where they've seen it misused, and what the cross says to both.

memoryVerse.text: And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.

sessions.title: Lead Us Not, Deliver Us
sessions.aim: To end the study where prayer most often lives, in the dark, with the petitions about temptation and evil, and to face the hardest thing about prayer, the unanswered kind, without offering a tidy reason, learning the persistence that keeps asking when heaven is silent.
sessions.summary:
The prayer doesn't end on triumph. It ends asking for help: "And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil" (Matthew 6:13). It assumes the danger is real. That's honest, because it's where prayer lives for most of us, most of the time: not in bright assurance but in the dark, asking.

So we have to face the deepest objection any praying person carries. We've asked, specifically and faithfully, for help that didn't come, and the silence is the loudest argument against the whole thing. Many faithful people have prayed into that silence for months. The study won't hand anyone a tidy reason.

What it can do is hold up what Jesus did and didn't promise. He never promised a life without danger or an unanswered ask. He did teach a persistence that sounds almost rude. And in Gethsemane he prayed his own unanswered prayer: the cup didn't pass, and he prayed, "not as I will, but as you will." The study ends there, in the garden, with a Father who didn't remove the cup and never left.

keyScripture.why: "And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil" (Matthew 6:13). The prayer closes on a plea for help in real danger, not on triumph. It names the dark as the place prayer often lives and points to the persistence that keeps asking when no answer comes.

discussion.q: The prayer ends with "deliver us from evil," not with a note of victory. Why do you think Jesus closes it there?
discussion.behind: Notice the ending itself. We might expect assurance, and instead the prayer closes asking for help against evil. Let the room feel how true that is to where prayer actually lives. For people who are struggling, it's a relief.

discussion.q: If you're willing, name a prayer you prayed faithfully that wasn't answered the way you asked. What has the silence done to your praying?
discussion.behind: Make room for the hardest thing and don't hurry past it. Most people carry an unanswered prayer that has quietly worn down their confidence. Let it be said without explaining it away. Don't offer a reason. And don't press anyone to share; some of these are too fresh.

discussion.q: Read Luke 11:5-8 and 18:1-8. Jesus commends a persistence that sounds almost rude. Why does he tie prayer to persistence instead of to one faithful asking?
discussion.behind: We tend to ask once and read silence as no. Jesus commands repeated asking. Luke 18:1 gives the reason: "that they ought always to pray and not lose heart." Help the room see that the parables work by contrast. God isn't the grumpy neighbor or the corrupt judge. The persistence is a child refusing to stop coming.

discussion.q: Does the lack of a neat answer to unanswered prayer make faith harder to hold, or oddly more believable, for you?
discussion.behind: Let the room sit with the refusal to explain. A neat answer often wounds real grief. Some will find the honesty steadying and some will find it hard; both are fine to say out loud.

discussion.q: Read Matthew 26:36-44. Jesus asked three times for the cup to pass, and it didn't. How does it change your unanswered prayers to know the Son prayed one too?
discussion.behind: End the study in the garden, without resolving it. Gethsemane doesn't explain our silence, but Christ has been in it. Answer first with your own unanswered prayer if you can. Leave the room there, with a Father who didn't remove the cup and didn't leave.

objections.objection: Prayer doesn't work. I've prayed for years for things any good father would give, healing, a marriage saved, a child brought home, and nothing came. The silence is the strongest argument that no one is on the other end.
objections.response: This is the most painful objection in the room, and it shouldn't get a glib answer. The tidy reasons, it wasn't the right time, you lacked faith, God had a better plan, usually wound more than they heal. Here is what Jesus did and didn't promise. He never promised a life without the dark or without an unanswered prayer. In Gethsemane he asked the Father to let the cup pass, and it didn't. If unanswered prayer proves no one is listening, then no one was listening to the Son of God in the garden, and the faith denies that. The silence isn't proof of absence. Sometimes it's the hardest form of a presence that doesn't do what we asked and doesn't leave. And three days after the garden, the no turned out not to be the end of the story.

objections.objection: If God already knows what's best and will do his will anyway, why pray at all? And why does Jesus tell me to keep asking like the widow pestering the judge? That makes prayer sound like wearing God down.
objections.response: Luke says Jesus told that parable so that "they ought always to pray and not lose heart" (Luke 18:1). The persistence is for us. Jesus isn't suggesting we wear down a reluctant God; the parable works by contrast. If even a corrupt judge finally answers someone who keeps coming, how much more will a good Father. So why keep asking? Because prayer isn't mainly a way to change God's mind. It's the relationship in which we're changed, kept close, and kept coming. We don't keep asking to inform God or overpower him. We keep asking because a child who trusts his father keeps coming to him.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What's the prayer you stopped praying because it was never answered, and what would it take to bring it to God again, even without a guarantee?
sessions.practice: This week, take up one prayer you gave up on because the silence wore you out, and pray it again each day, without demanding an answer or a timeline. Pray it the way the widow kept coming, not to wear God down but to keep coming to him. On the hardest day, when it feels like praying into a ceiling, pray the words from the garden, "not as I will, but as you will," and stay with God a little longer than feels comfortable. Write down what it was like to return to a prayer you'd abandoned.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we've prayed into silence, some of us for years, and we've wondered whether anyone was there. Tonight we bring you the prayers you didn't answer as well as the ones you did: the healing that didn't come, the person who didn't come back, the rescue we begged for and didn't see. We don't understand the silence, and we won't pretend we do. But your Son prayed in a garden for a cup to pass, and it didn't, and you didn't leave him, and that wasn't the end of his story. Lead us not into temptation. Deliver us from evil. And where you don't deliver us the way we asked, stay with us. Teach us to keep coming to you in the dark. Not our will, but yours. Amen.
reflection: What unanswered prayer has worn down my confidence, and have I ever brought the silence itself to God instead of just dropping the request?
Is my asking a way of trying to wear God down, or a way of refusing to leave him in the dark?
If Christ prayed an unanswered prayer in Gethsemane and the Father didn't leave him, what does that say about my own unanswered prayers?
sessions.teaching:
The prayer doesn't end where we might want it to. We might want a high note, the kingdom secured and the table set. Instead it ends with a plea for help: "And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil" (Matthew 6:13). The ending takes for granted the very things we wish prayer would let us skip. It assumes there's temptation real enough to fear and evil real enough to need rescue from. It doesn't promise those things away. It asks for help in the middle of them. I think Jesus ends here on purpose, because this is where prayer lives for most of us, most of the time. Not in bright certainty. In the dark, asking.

So we have to finish by facing the hardest thing about prayer, the thing every person who prays carries and few say out loud. Sometimes prayer doesn't seem to work. You've prayed, not casually but specifically and faithfully, for years, for things any good father would surely give. Healing for a body that kept declining. A marriage you begged God to save that ended anyway. A child you've asked him every day to bring home who hasn't come home. And nothing came. The silence after a prayer like that is the loudest argument against the whole enterprise. It says no one is on the other end.

I'm not above that. Many faithful people have prayed into that silence for months with no sense that anyone was listening, and I won't hand you a tidy reason that wraps your grief in a bow. The tidy reasons are usually worse than the silence. It wasn't the right time. You didn't have enough faith. God had a better plan. Said to someone in real anguish, each of those lands like a slap, because each finds a way to make the suffering the sufferer's fault or to turn God's silence into a clever strategy.

What I can do is hold up what Jesus actually did and didn't promise. He never promised that the faithful would be spared temptation, evil, darkness, or unanswered prayer. The prayer he taught assumes the opposite. And then there's what I've come to believe is the deepest comfort for anyone praying in silence, though it doesn't explain anything. Jesus prayed an unanswered prayer himself. The night before he died, in the garden of Gethsemane, he fell on his face and prayed, "My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will" (Matthew 26:39). Luke says that in his agony "his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground" (Luke 22:44). Matthew tells us he prayed three times. And the cup didn't pass.

If an unanswered prayer proves no one is listening, then no one was listening to Jesus in the garden, and the faith falls apart. But the faith doesn't say that. It says the Father heard every word and loved his Son completely and didn't take the cup away, because the cup was the rescue of the world, and in that dark hour not even the Son was shown what the no was for. The silence wasn't absence. It was the hardest form of a presence that wouldn't do what was asked and wouldn't leave. Notice how Jesus prayed it through: "not as I will, but as you will." That isn't giving up. It's trust holding on to the Father exactly when the Father isn't doing what was asked.

Now hear what Jesus teaches about praying when the answer doesn't come, because it isn't what you'd expect. He doesn't say ask once and accept the silence. He tells of a man who pounds on his neighbor's door at midnight until he gets bread (Luke 11:5-8), and of a widow who keeps coming back to an unjust judge until he gives in. Luke tells us why: "that they ought always to pray and not lose heart" (Luke 18:1). That's a persistence that sounds almost rude. And it isn't because God is the grumpy neighbor or the corrupt judge. The parables work by contrast. If even they answer someone who keeps coming, how much more will a good Father.

The persistence, then, is for us. C. S. Lewis wrote about the puzzles of asking God for things with unusual candor and didn't pretend them away. Keeping on asking is the relationship staying alive through the silence. It's the child who doesn't get the answer and still doesn't stop coming, because the staying close, the refusing to walk off into the dark alone, is much of what prayer was always for. And even when we can't find words, Paul says, "the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words" (Romans 8:26).

So this study doesn't get a triumphant ending, and I won't give it one, because that would be lying about what we've been studying. The prayer Jesus taught ends in a garden in the dark, asking for rescue that may not come the way we asked, holding on to a Father who hears every word, who doesn't always take the cup away, and who has promised in Christ never to leave. Lead us not into temptation. Deliver us from evil. And where you don't deliver us the way we begged, stay. We'll keep asking. We won't pray it alone, because the Son prayed it first, and on the far side of his unanswered prayer was a morning no one in that garden could have imagined.

scriptureStudy.note: "And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil." The prayer ends asking for help against real danger, not on triumph, naming evil as something the praying life truly contends with.
"My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will." Jesus prays his own unanswered prayer and trusts the Father's will through it.

"And he told them a parable to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart." Luke states the purpose plainly. Persistence is the answer to the discouragement of slow or silent answers.

The friend at midnight keeps knocking until the bread is given. Jesus commends bold persistence, not because God is reluctant but to teach us to keep coming. The contrast shows how much more a good Father will answer.

"Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, that it should leave me. But he said to me, 'My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.'" Paul's prayer is answered with a no that isn't abandonment: grace inside the trouble rather than the trouble removed.

A lament that ends in darkness, with no resolution; its last line is "my companions have become darkness" (Psalm 88:18). Scripture keeps a prayer that doesn't resolve, so a dark prayer isn't a failure of faith.

"Likewise the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words." Even our wordless, worn-out praying is taken up and carried.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, take up the biblical tradition of lament, which much of the modern church has lost. Its loss is part of why unanswered prayer so easily becomes a crisis of faith instead of an act of it. About a third of the Psalms are laments, prayers of complaint, protest, and unanswered ache, and some don't resolve. Psalm 88 ends with darkness. Walter Brueggemann, in The Message of the Psalms (1984) and in a 1986 essay on "the costly loss of lament," argued that a church permitted only praise loses the ability to tell the truth about suffering, and that the laments keep the relationship with God honest when life falls apart.

Set that beside the assumption that a faithful prayer is an upbeat one and that complaint means failing faith, and ask what's lost when the church gives people no permission to pray in the dark. Then weigh how lament is itself an act of faith: you don't complain to a God you think is absent. Bringing the silence and the grief and the unanswered request back to God is a refusal to let go of him. Gethsemane stands at the center of it, where "not as I will, but as you will" isn't the abandonment of the request but its surrender into trust.

memoryVerse.text: And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.

leaderPrimer:
Assume from the first minute that almost everyone in your group is a little ashamed of how they pray. They think everyone else got a script they missed. Some have faked warmth in group prayer for years. Some begged God for one thing, once, with everything they had, and the silence that followed is still the loudest thing in their faith. So the danger in leading five weeks on prayer is plain. You can turn prayer into one more performance the strugglers fail at, a skill with experts and a standard the room measures itself against and goes home smaller. Don't. When the disciples asked to be taught, Jesus gave them a prayer a child can memorize, and this study walks it slowly on purpose.

The first session touches a wound. For some people in your room the word Father isn't a comfort but a bruise, because theirs left, or never came, or stayed and hurt them. Say so in session one, out loud. It tells the wounded that the prayer rests on adoption, on what God has done, and not on what they manage to feel.

Handle session four with both hands. Someone at your table may have been told they must forgive an abuser on command or lose God's mercy. Say plainly that the clause describes what grace does in a forgiven heart, that it isn't a transaction, that forgiveness isn't the same as trust or reconciliation, that it can take years, and that God is patient with the slowness. If anyone is still in danger, their safety comes first, and the help on this page is there for that.

When the unanswered prayer comes up, and it will, don't defend God. Point to the garden, where the Son asked for the cup to pass and then carried it. At the end of each night, pray plainly: short, true, and unembarrassed. People will forget most of what you explain and remember what it sounded like when someone stopped performing and talked to the Father. Then keep praying yourself, dry weeks included. This prayer is learned by praying it.

faq.q: Is this study going to make me feel guilty about how little or how poorly I pray?
faq.a: No, and it works hard not to. The whole study rests on the conviction that prayer is a child speaking to a Father, not a performance to be graded. If you came braced to be told you're doing it wrong, you'll find a study that treats your thin or struggling prayer life as the right place to start, and that stays with you in the dry months and the silence instead of scolding you for them.

faq.q: Why is the whole study built on the Lord's Prayer instead of teaching about prayer in general?
faq.a: Because when the disciples asked Jesus to teach them to pray, he didn't give them principles. He gave them this prayer (Luke 11:1-4; Matthew 6:9-13). Each clause trains something. "Our Father" teaches who we pray to. "Hallowed be your name" and "your kingdom come" reorder what we want. "Give us this day" teaches dependence. "Forgive us... as we also have forgiven" is where mercy received becomes mercy given. "Lead us not" and "deliver us" are prayer in the dark. Walking the prayer one petition at a time is slower and more concrete than a survey of prayer, and it lets the words Jesus actually gave do the teaching.

faq.q: I struggle to call God Father because of my own father. Is this study going to force that word on me?
faq.a: No, and session one is built for you. It takes the wound seriously. The distinction it offers is that God isn't your earthly father made bigger. He's the Father your earthly father was meant to reflect and didn't, so the failures of the one don't define the other. And prayer doesn't begin with a warm feeling you have to produce. It begins with something given: in Christ you've been adopted. You can say the word before you feel it, the way a child learns a name he never got to use.

faq.q: Does praying "hallowed be your name" mean God needs us to flatter him before he'll help?
faq.a: No. A God who needed our applause to feel secure wouldn't be worth praying to, and the instinct that recoils from that picture is a healthy one. But the hallowing is for us, not for him. God gains nothing when his name is honored, the way a mountain gains nothing when you admire it. The human heart always puts something first, and when it puts anything but God there, it breaks under a weight that thing can't carry. To pray "hallowed be your name" is to ask God to put first in you what is actually first. Session two works this through.

faq.q: Why pray for daily bread when I can just buy food at the store?
faq.a: Because the petition was never mainly about bread. It's about who you believe keeps you alive. You can buy the food, but you didn't grow the wheat, you didn't give yourself the strength to earn the paycheck, and you didn't make your heart beat this morning. The grocery store doesn't end our dependence. It hides it behind a long supply chain. The word "daily" matters too. It echoes the manna in the wilderness, which spoiled when people hoarded it (Exodus 16:20), and it trains an anxious heart to trust God for today. Session three takes this up, and it's careful to say that the prayer doesn't forbid saving or planning.

faq.q: Does "forgive us... as we forgive" mean God's forgiveness depends on my forgiving others first?
faq.a: Read as a transaction, it would be monstrous, and session four refuses that reading. The "as" isn't a price you pay to earn God's mercy. It's a sign of whether his mercy has reached you. A heart that has really been forgiven starts to forgive, the way ice that has been warmed begins to drip. That's a world away from telling a wounded person to forgive on command or be damned. The study is careful to say that forgiveness isn't pretending the wound didn't happen, isn't handing trust back to someone who hasn't changed, and isn't giving up on justice or safety. For the deeply wounded it may take years, and God is patient with that.

faq.q: Is forgiving someone the same as saying what they did was okay?
faq.a: No, it's close to the opposite. Forgiveness starts by naming the debt as real: the harm was genuine and the wrong was wrong. Only then does it choose not to make the other person pay what they owe. The debt doesn't disappear. Someone bears it, and in forgiveness it's the one who was wronged. That's why it costs so much, and it's the shape of the cross, where the one who owed nothing bore what the guilty owed. You aren't letting anyone off the hook. You're taking the hook into your own hand, and you can still seek justice and keep yourself safe while you do.

faq.q: I've prayed for years and gotten silence. What does this study say about unanswered prayer?
faq.a: It says so without flinching and without a tidy reason. Session five refuses the answers that add to grief: it wasn't the right time, you lacked faith, God had a better plan. Each one finds a way to make the suffering your fault. Instead it points to what Jesus did. In Gethsemane he asked the Father to let the cup pass from him (Matthew 26:39), and it didn't pass, and the Father didn't leave him. If an unanswered prayer proved no one was listening, then no one heard the Son in the garden. The study doesn't explain the silence. It stays in it with you.

faq.q: If God is going to do his will anyway, why pray at all, and why does Jesus tell me to keep asking?
faq.a: Luke says Jesus told the parable of the persistent widow so that "they ought always to pray and not lose heart" (Luke 18:1). The persistence is for us. The parable works by contrast: if even a corrupt judge gives in to someone who keeps coming, how much more will a good Father hear his children. Prayer isn't mainly a way of changing God's mind. It's the relationship in which we're kept close. You keep asking because a child who trusts his father keeps coming, and the coming itself, answered or not, is much of what prayer is for.

faq.q: Does this study promise that if I learn to pray right, my prayers will be answered?
faq.a: No, and it refuses to on purpose. It ends in session five in a garden in the dark, because prayer this side of heaven doesn't get a clean resolution, and a study that promised one would be lying. Some prayers are answered as they were asked. Some are answered with a no that isn't abandonment. Some are met with grace that's enough inside a trouble God doesn't remove, as Paul found (2 Corinthians 12:8-9). What the study offers isn't a method that works. It's a Father you keep coming to, in the light and in the dark.

faq.q: Why does the study keep admitting the writer's and the leader's own struggle with prayer?
faq.a: Because nobody learns to pray from someone standing above them. The study doesn't pretend anyone has prayer mastered. It owns the prayers that seem to hit the ceiling, the dry months, the times we pray "your kingdom come" while building our own, and the times we pray "forgive us" while keeping a ledger. A leader who can say "I struggle with this too" sits beside the room instead of over it, and that's usually what gives everyone else permission to stop pretending.

faq.q: I'm a skeptic. Isn't prayer just talking to yourself and calling it God?
faq.a: It's a fair challenge. The study doesn't try to answer it by promising results. It spends a whole session on prayer that goes unanswered and refuses to explain the silence away. What it offers isn't proof but a claim worth weighing: that prayer is less a way of getting outcomes than a relationship with a Father, and that Jesus himself prayed a prayer that wasn't granted and kept praying. You can ask whether a faith willing to put its own unanswered prayer at the center is more believable than one that guarantees results. You won't be asked to pretend.

faq.q: How do I lead this if my own prayer life is a mess?
faq.a: A messy prayer life doesn't disqualify you. It may help. The study is built to be led by a fellow learner. Every discussion question carries notes on what it's after, and every session ends in prayer rather than advice, so you aren't improvising. What you need is to refuse to shame anyone for how they pray, to keep the room safe for the wounded and the doubting and the silent, to take special care in sessions one and four, and to point everyone, yourself first, to the One who taught us to pray and who prayed in the dark himself.

timeline.event: In the wilderness God feeds Israel with manna, a day's portion each morning. Kept overnight, it bred worms and stank (Exodus 16:20). It's the picture behind the request for daily bread.
The Psalms begin to take shape. About a third of them are laments, prayers of complaint and unanswered ache, and some, like Psalm 88, end in darkness without resolution.

Jesus teaches the Lord's Prayer in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 6:9-13) and again when a disciple asks, "Lord, teach us to pray" (Luke 11:1). The night before the cross he prays in Gethsemane that the cup might pass from him (Matthew 26:39).
Paul writes to the Romans that believers have received "the Spirit of adoption as sons" (Romans 8:15) and that the Spirit intercedes "with groanings too deep for words" (Romans 8:26).

Tertullian and then Cyprian of Carthage write the earliest surviving Christian commentaries on the Lord's Prayer. In parts of the early church the prayer was taught to new believers as they came to baptism, as the prayer of God's adopted family.

Augustine writes his Confessions, which opens by telling God that our heart is restless until it rests in him. In other works he describes sin as disordered love, loving lesser things above greater ones.

Martin Luther, who knew long seasons of spiritual dread he called Anfechtungen, writes A Simple Way to Pray for his barber, Peter Beskendorf, showing an ordinary believer how to pray the Lord's Prayer clause by clause.
John Calvin expounds the Lord's Prayer in his Institutes, from the first edition of 1536 to the last of 1559, where his chapter on prayer calls it the chief exercise of faith.
The Westminster Shorter Catechism closes by teaching the Lord's Prayer petition by petition as the rule for directing our prayers.
C. S. Lewis publishes Reflections on the Psalms (1958), and after his death Letters to Malcolm: Chiefly on Prayer (1964), which takes up the puzzles of asking God for things with unusual candor.
Walter Brueggemann publishes The Message of the Psalms, recovering lament as a faithful form of prayer.
Eugene Peterson publishes Answering God, on the Psalms as the school of prayer, where we learn to answer the God who speaks first.
Timothy Keller publishes Prayer: Experiencing Awe and Intimacy with God, drawing on Augustine, Luther, and Calvin on the Lord's Prayer.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thank you for being here. Prayer is harder to talk about honestly than almost anything, so it took some courage. Before we start, three things. First, this is a safe room. You can say here that you don't really know how to pray, or that you stopped years ago, or that you pray and feel nothing, or that the word Father is hard for you. Nobody's going to grade you or hand you a tip. Second, this isn't a technique for getting God to do things. We're learning to pray from Jesus, one clause at a time, and at the center of it is a Father, not a method. Third, I'm not teaching this from above. I've prayed into what felt like a ceiling, and I've gone long stretches saying the right words to a God who felt far away. We're learning this together. Tonight we're sitting with this part of the prayer Jesus gave us: ________. Let me read our passage, and then we'll sit with it for a moment before anyone says anything. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes, only honest ones.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked hard at what this part of the prayer says. Now let's bring it into the week ahead, into the ordinary mornings and the hard nights where we actually pray or don't. That's where this either matters or it doesn't.
facilitatorScript.close: We're going to stop there. If it doesn't feel settled, that's all right; prayer doesn't settle on a schedule, and I'm not going to pretend it does. Take this part of the prayer into your week. Try the practice, and sit with the reflection questions on your own. If the word Father is hard for you, or you're carrying a prayer you gave up on, or a hurt that the word forgive presses on, please don't carry it alone. Talk to me, or to someone safe in this room. Let me pray for us before we go. Thank you for the honesty it took to be here.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, agree that the room is safe and that no one will be shamed for how they pray, and pray the Lord's Prayer slowly as a group. Say plainly that for some people the word Father is a wound, and that this room is a safe place for that.
Week 2: Session 1, Our Father, with extra care for anyone for whom the word Father is hard.
Week 3: Session 2, Hallowed Be Your Name, Your Kingdom Come, with extra time on disordered desire and the small kingdoms we run.
Week 4: Session 3, Give Us This Day, on dependence and daily bread, with the manna in the wilderness.
Week 5: Session 4, part one, Forgive Us: sit first with how much we've been forgiven before turning to the forgiveness we give.
Week 6: Session 4, part two, As We Forgive: the cost of bearing a real debt, handled with great care for anyone deeply wounded.
Week 7: Session 5, Lead Us Not, Deliver Us: prayer in the dark, unanswered prayer, and the persistence Jesus asks of us.

Week 8: Pray the whole Lord's Prayer together clause by clause, look back over the five practices, and let each person name what they're carrying to the Father, with room for anyone who needs further help.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together: who we pray to, and the reordering of desire toward God's name and kingdom.
Week 2: Session 3, Give Us This Day, with extra time on the end of self-sufficiency.
Week 3: Session 4, Forgive Us, As We Forgive, handled with care for the wounded.
Week 4: Session 5, Lead Us Not, Deliver Us, on prayer in the dark and unanswered prayer, with a short close praying the whole prayer together.

cadences.name: As written (5 weeks)
plan: Week 2: Session 2, Hallowed Be Your Name, Your Kingdom Come.
Week 3: Session 3, Give Us This Day.
Week 4: Session 4, Forgive Us, As We Forgive.
Week 5: Session 5, Lead Us Not, Deliver Us.

glossary.definition: The prayer Jesus gave when his disciples asked him to teach them to pray, recorded in Matthew 6:9-13 and Luke 11:2-4. This study treats it as a school of prayer as well as a prayer to say, and walks it one clause at a time.

God's act of making people who weren't his children into his sons and daughters, with the right to call him Father (Romans 8:15). The study grounds the first words of the prayer here, so the fatherless can say Father because it's been given, not because they feel it.
The Aramaic word for father that Jesus used in prayer (Mark 14:36) and that the Spirit prompts in believers (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6). It's intimate without being careless.
Honoring God's name as holy, the first request of the prayer. In this study it isn't flattery God needs but a reordering the human heart needs, putting first in us what is already first.
Augustine's description of sin as loving lesser things more than greater ones, putting created goods where only the Creator belongs. Prayer, on this account, slowly puts our loves back in order.
God's reign, which the prayer asks to come "on earth as it is in heaven." To pray for it is to pray for a different king than yourself and to refuse to call any broken thing final.
The request for today's basic provision, asked one day at a time, echoing the manna in the wilderness. The study reads it as a confession that we don't keep ourselves alive.
The fact that we're made, not self-made, kept in being by God moment by moment. The study treats owning it as a relief rather than a humiliation.
Bonhoeffer's term, set against cheap grace, for grace that is free but was never cheap: it cost God his Son, and it calls the one who receives it to follow Christ.
Giving up the claim to make someone pay a real debt, and bearing the cost yourself. The study separates it from denial, from restored trust, and from giving up on justice or safety.

The biblical prayer of complaint, protest, and unanswered ache, which makes up about a third of the Psalms. Some laments don't resolve. The study treats lament as faithful prayer, not a failure of faith.
The garden where Jesus prayed the night before the cross, asking that the cup pass from him. The study makes it the center of what it says about unanswered prayer.

The keeping on asking that Jesus teaches in the parables of the friend at midnight (Luke 11:5-8) and the persistent widow (Luke 18:1-8). It isn't wearing down a reluctant God; it's a child who won't stop coming to the Father.
